cells.tense: You are here with what has grown, still holding the terms you set.
cells.act: set the finished thing down in a form that keeps
cells.ask: Write one arrangement that's working onto a single sheet — who gives what, who gets what — and put it where you'll both come across it.
cells.core:
What you've grown is steady, and the holding of it is a real act. You're bearing the terms of a fair exchange — who gives what, who receives — and it stays up because you keep choosing to hold it. That's endurance's quiet work at a harvest: not just collecting what came in, but carrying it.

The balancing is real and mostly unsaid, which means it leans on you being present to rebalance it. Put one working arrangement on a page where both of you can see it. The exchange is fair right now. A small written form lets it stay visible without you standing over it. Choose one, write it plainly, and set the page somewhere your days pass.
cells.sheetLine: What you've grown holds because you hold it.
cells.verb: receiving what is fair and giving what is fair in return
cells.place: where you bear the weight of what has already grown

cells.tense: You'll brace for a reckoning before the scales have even tipped.
cells.act: carry your own share, all of it
cells.ask: This week, carry your half of the exchange and nothing past it. Note what you actually do, not what you suspect is owed.
cells.core:
You're bracing for a fairness you can't see yet. The tally runs past the actual exchange — counting who owes what before anything is owed — and the bracing starts to feel like strength. Endurance under pressure is real; this pressure is mostly forecast.

This week, carry your half and close the tally behind you. Don't check whether the other side matched it. If something's genuinely off, you'll meet it once, on your own reserves, when the week closes. What you'll likely feel by day four is the proof that the reckoning was in your head, not in the exchange itself.
cells.sheetLine: The reckoning runs past the actual exchange.

cells.tense: You stood at the exchange with your hand out and your hand back.
cells.act: strike one thing from the list that does not serve
cells.ask: Watch one week of what you hand out and what returns. Find the item that doesn't feed you and cross it off. Keep the rest.
cells.core:
You stood at the exchange and gave, and what came back didn't reach you. You're still handing things out; little is arriving on the return side that you can feel. Endurance has been running low, which is why it reads as stiffness instead of strength.

Sharpen one distinction: most of what you hand out still matters, and one item on the list doesn't. Find it — the favour, the check-in, the obligation you keep from habit — and cross it off for one week. Keep the rest. What's starved doesn't need more pushed into it; it needs one clear thing removed so what's left can be felt again.
cells.sheetLine: You give, and not enough comes back to reach you.

cells.tense: You are keeping the exchange even, and calling it luck.
cells.act: hold two true things without declaring either
cells.ask: The next time you quietly even something up, hold both facts a moment — you did it, it needed doing — then keep them to yourself and move on.
cells.core:
You read an exchange fast and let it settle without scorekeeping, and that ease is the honest center of this. It runs through most days unnamed. What slips is your part in it: you adjust a share here, absorb a cost there, and the story says the arrangement simply works.

Hold two true things without declaring either. You bear more than you count, and the other person doesn't see it. Wear that privately for a month — no speech, no ledger shown — and watch whether the exchange still feels even once you've stopped calling it luck. Endurance is your seat; you can hold a piece of knowledge a while before it changes a word you say.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it even and call it nothing.

attempts.check: The draft claims this person is holding a fair arrangement steady under pressure; the record says only that fair exchange is in balance at Fruition, seated in endurance — it does not say what they are bearing or who else is carrying a share. A reader could rightly say the arrangement is private, not shared, and the ask would still work: putting your own share on paper teaches anyone where their accounting actually lands. The line that serves the writer more than the person is 'carrying your share is the fair thing' — cut it; the cell should offer a form, not a verdict.
